Eileen Orford  

This is an interesting and sensible book by the Chair of the Ethics Committee of the United Kingdom Council for Psychotherapy (UKCP). It was written to air, both for the professional and the patient, issues that may become increasingly pressing as people become freer to complain and to express their grievances. It addresses these issues as they relate to psychotherapy practice within the United Kingdom.

It may, however, have more academic than practical interest for the child psychotherapist. While the Association of Child Psychotherapists is mentioned as the only psychotherapeutic body to have received recognition from the Department of Health, the quite considerable differences in the ethical position of those who work with children are not even mentioned. Such issues importantly include the confidentiality of the child's material in relation to the parents, differences in the contract (with whom is this made?) and the highly complicated questions of suspicions of abuse that may arise in work with children.

The title of the book is, perhaps, misleading from this point of view and specificity to its work with adults would clarify its brief. Even more importantly, the title suggests that the book is about psychotherapy and those whose criteria would meet the criteria of the UKCP or the BCP (the British Confederation of Psychotherapists.) However, there are frequent references to counsellors and counselling, and in the appendices which detail the ethical codes of the UKCP and BCP there is the inclusion of the equivalent data from the British Association of Counselling (BAC). The author does not explain this inclusion of counselling or significant similarities or differences between counselling and psychotherapy. If the book is to include the quite wide counselling field, the title should have made this clear.

It is noticeable that some of the interesting examples refer specifically to those involved in counselling. Perhaps this is not surprising in view of ‘the current proliferation of counselling courses of different lengths and content [that] mean that individuals can complete a basic, academically orientated course and immediately move on the further qualification through a supervision course or become trainers without having had any real experience of therapeutic practice’ (p. 22).

Editorial

Judith Edwards and Mary Walker

Mary Walker

Mary Walker  

We are pleased to open this August 1999 edition of the journal with what we hope will be the first of a number of symposia on key concepts and where our thinking about them has reached today. In the spirit of the dictionary definition of a symposium as ‘a convivial meeting’, we offer this collection of opinions on various aspects of the subject of ‘frustration’, and we hope that, by having a public forum for diverse views, we continue the tradition of engendering respect for difference. The authors, Anne Alvarez, Anne Harrison and Edna O'Shaughnessy, all from London, have contributed their conceptual and technical thoughts on frustration, and we hope these may stimulate correspondence in future editions.

The next two papers from South Africa also represent a new departure in terms of our wish to reflect on the nature and scope of work around the world. In ‘Home thoughts from abroad’, Sheila Miller from Johannesburg offers an impressionistic account of life in South Africa and a description of her consultation work in a township community centre. She opens up the debate as to whether psychoanalytically informed thinking and practice are appropriate in the South African milieu. Her reflections at the end of the paper about the role of the ancestors in South African culture and links with psychoanalytic thinking lead naturally on to Suzanne Maiello's paper, ‘Encounter with an African healer’. The author, who lives in Rome, had the fascinating opportunity to meet with a healer while on a three months' stay in South Africa. She extends further, in a thought-provoking analysis, the debate about both the possibilities and limits of cross-cultural psychotherapy, and indicates the need for psychoanalytic thinking to be open to the findings of interdisciplinary research, particularly in the area of anthropology.

The clinical section begins with ‘The suffering of Asperger children’, by Judy Shuttleworth, who has made a major contribution to the work of integrating recent research on both infant behaviour and brain development with psychodynamic thinking.

Editorial

Judith Edwards and Mary Walker

Mary Walker

Mary Walker  

What we call the beginning is often the end

and to make an end is to make a beginning.

The end is where we start from.1

(T.S. Eliot, Four Quartets)

Seldom have T.S. Eliot's words seemed more relevant as we stand at the juncture between two millennia, and this year has also seen the fiftieth anniversary of our Association, where we stand on the brink of a new era of change and development (see Lush, Hurst and Radford, Vol. 25 No. 1 of this journal). We are marking this turning point with a subsection on endings in this last journal of the twentieth century where the issues of loss and of gain are explored both theoretically and clinically. The second, Italian subsection serves also both as a review of past achievements in Italy, an indication of the work being undertaken there, and as a new venture for the journal with overviews of work around the world. (The August 2000 edition will feature work from Australia, and there are already further international editions being planned.)

But to begin with endings: our first paper by Isca Wittenberg: ‘Ending therapy, highlights the universal difficulty with endings which has been reflected in an absence of opportunities in training to grapple with these fundamental difficulties. The author describes the seminars she ran on endings at the Tavistock Clinic and gives a comprehensive overview, with clinical illustrations, of the issues which emerge and of the different ways in which endings occur and are dealt with.

Patsy Ryz and Jilian Wilson

Jilian Wilson

36 Essex Park
London N3 1NE

Jilian Wilson   Jilian Wilson worked as a psychiatric social worker with children and families in both London and New York before training as a child psychotherapist at the Tavistock Clinic and as an adult psychotherapist at the British Association of Psychotherapists. She has maintained an interest in applied work, and in 1990 took the opportunity to join a developing child and adolescent psychiatry department in a district general hospital after working for many years in the community child and family consultation service (child guidance).
Beginnings; endings; negative elasticity; boundaries; decision making; Hooke's Law; non-autistic shapes; too-good mothering; bifocal vision.

The paper describes an application of child psychotherapy in a paediatric setting. It examines the crucial part that attention to endings played in a clinical intervention where the phantasy of going on for ever threatened to inhibit growth. Case material is used to illustrate the different meanings and functions of endings and their significance in terms of parenting issues and developmental tasks. In this context the concept of negative elasticity is put forward as a useful tool for exploring the nature of boundaries. The final part of the paper focuses on the value of the external-reality experience of ending, its relationship to potential professional omnipotence and the importance of sustaining a tension between inner- and outer-world factors.

Lynda Miller   Lynda Miller works as a child psychotherapist in a child guidance clinic in North London, and also for the Tavistock Clinic in the adolescent department as joint head of the Learning Disability Service. She teaches on pre-clinical and clinical training courses at the Tavistock and in Bologna, Italy.

Gianna, could you tell us how the idea of taking the Tavistock Model Observation Course to Italy first arose?

I had been teaching in Rome at the Faculty of Child Neuro-Psychiatry, both lecturing and taking seminars. I met a number of people who wished, at some point, to come to London to train at the Tavistock. One of them asked me whether it would be possible to take at least part of the course there in Italy. For instance, when I was in Rome, could I take a work discussion seminar for people who may later wish to come to London? This made me think that, if it were possible to start one seminar of the ‘Observation Course’ in Italy, it may be possible to start the whole course, a course which I was familiar with because I was already teaching in it here at the Tavistock.

So how was the first Tavistock Model Observation Course in Italy set up? The first observation course started in October 1976. I spoke about it with Martha Harris in the spring of 1976. She was very enthusiastic about the idea and we thought together of a model that would reproduce the ‘Observation Course’ in a different country ‘under a different sky’, but with exactly the same number of seminars, the same amount of written work and also, and this is something Martha Harris felt rather strongly about, with the same teachers teaching here in London involved in the teaching in Rome.

Emanuela Quagliata   Emanuela Quagliata attended the Tavistock course in observational studies in London and the child psychotherapy training in Rome. She is a member of the Tavistock Society of Psychotherapists (TSP), of the Italian Association of Child Psychoanalytical Psychotherapy (AIPPI) and a member of the Italian Society of Psychoanalysis (SPI). She is currently registered on the doctorate course in psychoanalytic psychotherapy at the Tavistock Clinic, and carries out her research in Rome.
Omnipotent phantasy, pathological projective identification; loss; mourning.

In this paper I reflect on the phase of the analytic process which precedes the termination of a psychoanalysis and describe my work with an adolescent girl. Adolescents with serious eating disorders relive in a particularly violent way, in the final phase of their analysis, the catastrophic anxiety of separation and the fear of annihilation connected with this. The perception of the final date, felt to be irrevocable, reactivates in these patients the psychotic part of their personality, which tries through a phantasy of omnipotent possession (expressed through pathological projective identification) to obscure the reality of separateness and loss. It is useful with these patients to set a date for ending at least a year in advance to enable the working through of these psychotic anxieties. Clinical material illustrates how in the final year of treatment all phases of the analytic process are relived in a violent way, and how this emotional turbulence manifests itself as a battle between omnipotent phantasy and an increasing insight into psychic reality.

On the cover, this book states itself to be the first of a series which seeks to make the work of the Tavistock available to a wide audience in a clear readable style. It comes at a rime when child and adolescent psychotherapists in the community are struggling to deliver a service to children and young people who have suffered trauma and abuse and the kind of mental pain that is described here, within the financial constraints and long waiting lists of the modern National Health Service, with its current stress on evidence-based practice and throughput. The prejudice might be that a book describing clinical work in a prestigious institution would not reflect current experience in the community. That this book gives a vivid picture of how it is to approach this work, and the complexities and difficulties that get in the way, is a great achievement.

It is less successful in the explanations of theory and technique which are of interest to the student of psychotherapy, but, because of their complexity, are less accessible to the general reader. The theory is proudly in the Kleinian tradition. I think that at this time when there is still such suspicion of psychoanalysis and when child psychotherapists are being replaced by other professions, it would add richness as well as being politic to include other theoretical traditions and their current development.

The deepest impression on the reader is that of the pain of the children whose stories we hear and that of their parents and families, glimpsed in the background. The psychotic states of the tide are understood as a communication by their therapists. Emotional understanding is explained as the way the children are helped to emerge from long-established retreats into bizarre behaviour patterns, to resume their development and place in school or college and attempt to establish normal relationships. The understanding of how early environmental failure has contributed to the confused inner world of these children is conveyed not as something blameworthy, but in a spirit of concern at what is a transgenerational issue, as so often with abuse.

Letter to the Editors from Noela Byrne, Kerry Gee, George Haralambous, Maria Kourt, Mee Mee Lee and Norma Tracey, Sydney, Australia

It seems that Shuttleworth's dilemma (Journal of Child Psychotherapy 25(1)) echoes the same problem with which health professionals in Sydney have had to grapple. It is the struggle to adjust a way of dunking into a psychosocial milieu which does not value it as the ‘one and only’, or even as having any value at all. With the advent of evidence-based strategies, the emphasis is on numbers and identifying target populations with a degree of need in the community rather than a degree of need in the individual child or adult. These could be considered opposing forces. However, it is the task of health professionals utilizing psychoanalytic thinking to understand this as a normal tension of their professional lives and to find a ‘good enough’ balance for the needs of the individual and the community. Part of this struggle involves keeping alive the practice of child psychotherapy.

The practice of child psychotherapy in Sydney, NSW, is established in a very different way from that in the United Kingdom. The role of the child psychotherapist is hardly, acknowledged by the NSW Department of Health so that those working in the area of child mental health are employed to work genetically as social workers, psychologists, occupational therapists and child psychiatrists. Some of these health professionals would have had an exposure to the analytic way of working either in their training or during their professional life. Being thus analytically informed may lead them to choose child psychotherapy as one of their preferred ways of working. However, because their training is not in ‘pure’ child psychotherapy or psychoanalysis, the struggles discussed by Shuttleworth facing the district child psychotherapist and the question of ‘dual citizenship’ is not a burning issue.

Pat Radford

Pat Radford

14 Ferncroft Avenue

Pat Radford  

These are some of the random memories of happenings and events linked in my mind with the ACP for approximately the last thirty years. There are so many many people, and I am naming very few but all of the recalls are populated.

18

Early Beginnings

I became aware of the importance in my professional life of the ACP when I attended my first study weekend (1962) – one of the many initiative occasions which cemented the unity of the Association. These yearly meetings, taking place at the Hampstead Child Therapy Course & Clinic (renamed the Anna Freud Centre on Miss Freud's death), were exciting, exhilarating events with presentation of high-quality papers by members of each training school, followed by intense discussions in which semantics added to the wonderful learning confusion (what were the definitions of introjection/projection?). All continued as we ate and drank, with our amazing appetites, the delicious food and drink provided by the members. We were asking to bring our favourite dish, yet there was always a balance of savoury and sweet – could this have been symbolic of the diversity in our unity? They were ‘getting to know you’ gatherings, and the beginnings of long-lasting friendships in our small community – fewer than 100 members. As the membership has increased, we outgrew the original venue, moving to the Tavistock, to the Business School, and onwards, being however still provided with diverse, often brilliant papers and usually excellently catered food; but it is more difficult now for the ‘oldies' to keep in touch with the many new faces.

I cannot remember when (perhaps in 1968) I was ‘coerced’ into standing for the Executive Committee and found myself involved in a series of sub-committees for many years. I do remember Doris Wills, one of the original founders of the Association, the clear authority on any constitutional matter, kindly instructing us all on what could be done legally, cutting through our too frequent hazy proposals. Jess Guthrie was the convener of my first ‘investigative’ sub-committee which tried to define ethics but it was constantly side-tracked, with good humour, by the problems of a growing organization. Margaret Hurst was its long-suffering minuting secretary. The regular meetings sometimes took place in my flat, as have so many committees. I learnt how to have the limited refreshments in place before the meetings and after my patient's departure. I wonder why (interpretations galore!) I thought that both committee members and patients had some fixation in the oral phase which needed to be concretely contained. I was consultant supervisor at the Sophia Hospital in Rotterdam for many years and the Dutch butter cake was a firm favourite at the meetings.

This paper discusses the changing working environment of child psychotherapists in the public sector in the UK whose responsibility is to play a part in providing a general service to a local community. It suggests they operate with a kind of dual citizenship, owing allegiance both to the psychoanalytic community and to the public sector. Transitions between one and the other are demanding, requiring careful thought and management This has become more demanding because of changes occurring within the public sector as a whole and within multidisciplinary, multi-approach child and adolescent mental health teams. The nature of these changes is outlined. It is suggested that their cumulative effect is radical and irreversible and that, if district child psychotherapy is to be sustained, it will need to adapt to them in ways that are understood by and are acceptable to both the psychoanalytic and the public-sector communities. Hard thinking will be needed to carry forward into the next fifty years the achievements of district child psychotherapy in the UK in its first fifty years.

Janet Shaw  

In this book Eric Rhode researches into the area of human experience described by John Milton in Paradise Lost as the ‘rising world of waters dark and deep won from the void and formless infinite’. He is predominantly influenced by W. R. Bion's later works in which Bion struggles to formulate a description of ineffable experience which he names simply ‘O’. He contrasts two global points of view, the medical and the religious vertices, described by Bion. The medical vertex focuses on explanation and is intolerant of gaps in understanding which it seeks to fill with one concept after another to create an illusion of a continuity in knowledge, as if this could be possible. The medical vertex is grounded in linear and sequential logical thinking to the exclusion of all other aspects of experience.

The religious vertex embraces uncertainty and unknowability as fundamental and not as obstacles to overcome. Chaos takes on a significance from which meaning may emerge but ultimately it is unfathomable and can only be partially and incompletely known. The becoming of ‘O’ describes the emergence of meaning from this state of not knowing and Eric Rhode seeks to illuminate this as a main theme in his book. He takes Bion's scene of a tennis court as a metaphor for the stripping away of existing concepts in order to gain access into this area of experience: the ‘waters dark and deep’. Bion suggests that a beam of darkness is brought to bear on the tennis court scene so that the couple playing tennis disappear and the focus narrows to the net until only a hole in the net is visible. Any conceptual understanding of the scene is lost in the process and the emotional focus is removed from the primal scene of the couple. The pre-Oedipal anxieties of not knowing and consequent disintegration arise in the gap or hole leading to feelings of terror and a dread of annihilation.

Lynn Champion  

Bracken and Petty have put together a series of articles about the proliferation of psychological ‘aid’ based on Western psychological models, in particular of Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder, to peoples exposed to war and violence. They provide us with a series of articles by doctors, NGO policy makers and academics who have direct experience of working with people who have suffered from war. This collection is clear-sighted, well argued, intelligent and thought provoking. The authors give us a serious analysis of modern war, usually internecine, along with a view of the different ways war is experienced from the perspective of specific cultures. They describe the effect on local communities, children and women. They analyse the Western model of Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) and argue about its relevance for helping these peoples.

I am impressed by the lucid way in which all these authors inter-link their experience and knowledge with theoretical analysis. They also enable us to gain some inkling of, to imagine or empathize with local people, suspending for a while the perspective of the ‘expert’ and the constraints of our own Western identity.

Modern war or combat is increasingly waged against the very fabric of a society. Summerfield's social analysis gives us a deeper understanding of how this is experienced and its impact on communities. We also learn about the social responses to war, torture and exile. Social roles of memory and meaning are discussed and shown to be in contradistinction to psychiatric ideas of traumatic memory. The deconstruction of the concept of PTSD by Bracken is both timely and courageous. The idea of PTSD has become so prolific that it is refreshing to be shown that it is actually symbiotic with the Western conception of the individual. This, along with psychological cognitivism, is contrasted with social connectedness, which in many societies replaces personal achievement. Such a cultural difference has considerable implications for psychosocial programmes.

These three articles describe the establishment and growth of the Association of Child Psychotherapists over the last fifty yean, 1949-99. Dora Lush outlines the early roots of the Association and its gradual emergence from a sub-committee of the British Psychological Society. It became the Provisional Association of Child Psychotherapists (Non-Medical) in 1949 and the Association of Child Psychotherapists (ACP) in 1951, with ‘non-medical’ being dropped in 1972. This book is a collection of papers produced by members of the Adolescent Department of the Tavistock Clinic. It is edited by Robin Anderson and Anna Dartington who have both also produced two of the strongest papers in the book. By its very nature, as a collection of separate papers, the book is uneven in its quality. Some of the papers give the impression of having been written primarily for some other occasion and having then had their emphasis slightly altered to make them suitable for this book. This may, of course, not be the case. It may be that the wish to show the wide spectrum of ‘adolescent disturbance’ and the diversity of the work being carried out at times leaves this collection feeling rather disparate, without a unifying focus. Some major areas of adolescent disturbance such as drug addiction or delinquent behaviour are merely mentioned, but not addressed in detail. That said, this is a worthwhile and immensely readable book, full of descriptions of careful and painstaking work, with clinical vignettes which bring the troubled adolescent vividly in front of us and with a solid theoretical base, rooted for the most part in post-Kleinian thinking, which underpins the work undertaken.

The introduction by Anderson and Dartington uses the history of the Adolescent Department to set the theme of adolescence in context, within both literature and the outside world. Anna Dartington's paper, which begins the book, is written with such warmth and humanity it makes the reader eager for more.

The title of the book is taken from Macbeth. Malcolm urges Macduff, on receiving the news of the brutal slaughter of his wife and children:

… ne'er pull your hat upon your brows;

Give sorrow words. The grief that does not speak

Whispers the o'er fraught heart and bids it break

This second edition of Judd's book, first published in 1989, offers a highly sensitive account of clinical work with a dying child in the context of an astute and masterly discussion and review of the theoretical debates about working with terminally ill children and young people. Through the rigorous and meticulous uncovering of the research and fuller understanding of death, of the moral and ethical issues raised by certain treatments for life-threatening illness, the reader is opened to a deeply distressing experience, while at the same time feeling contained by the detailed exposition and attempts to understand the grief and sense of loss, mourning and outrage that the death of a child brings. The attempt to find words for the sorrow that the dying child, and those involved with him, experience is ever-present.

There are eight years between the publications of the first and second editions of the book. The salient issues in working with the seriously ill, the disabled and the dying remain under the microscope in this second edition. Judd considers when defences are useful and when they are maladaptive; how the chronically ill child can work through the normal developmental phases, especially adolescence, with its thrust towards independence and autonomy, when illness or disability makes him dependent on adults for basic care. She asks the anguished question about the point beyond which life should be sustained by medical intervention and how we evaluate the quality of the remaining life for a child whose death is prolonged. She looks at the crucial issues around the care of dying children and young people and the need for the therapist to learn to ‘acknowledge the “not knowing” about the meaning of death, nor when it will come, to a particular child or his family’. The overall aim is to encompass dying children's preoccupations and the climate in which they find themselves.

This paper follows the progress of intensive psychoanalytic psychotherapy offered to a severely abused and deprived 5–year-old boy in the first eighteen months of treatment. It attempts to show how certain adjustments to technique need to be considered to allow such a traumatized child to benefit from the held that is available. When a young child has encountered profound setbacks to early developmental processes the work in therapy must account for the absences of more ordinary communication and the presence of features which are full of mistrust and emotional bleakness. The role and the personality of the therapist are challenged in ways which demand an approach which may be considered unusually active in order to try to shape some meaning for the child without an emotional vocabulary.

Judith Edwards and Mary Walker

Mary Walker

Mary Walker  

The last year of this millennium coincides with the fiftieth anniversary of the setting up of the Association of Child Psychotherapists, and in this edition we mark the occasion by publishing a history of the association's evolution, followed by a selection of papers which, we hope, reflect the breadth, scope and quality of the work we undertake around the world.

We open with an article by three authors which describes the establishment and growth of the Association as well as giving a personal commentary on the experience of being an active member of an expanding profession. Dora Lush describes the emergence of the ACP from a sub-committee via a provisional association (‘non-medical’) to a fully fledged Association. Margaret Hurst takes up the account, focusing on the last decade from 1989 to 1999 where there has been an increasing professionalization of the ACP and its activities. Finally, Pat Radford gives a personal account, tinged with humour and exasperation, of her own participation in this journey.

The second paper, ‘Finding new clinical pathways in the changing world of district child psychotherapy’, takes the discussion forward. The author Alan Shuttleworth reflects on the need for hard thinking in order to take the achievements of child psychotherapy in the community over the last fifty years forward into the next millennium. While the author is describing the professional landscape in Great Britain, these changes can also be seen to be reflected in the profession around the world, as psychoanalytic psychotherapy responds to the need to change and adapt while remaining true to its core thinking. We hope this paper will promote a debate with overseas colleagues, and we would welcome comments from practitioners around the world, to contribute to an international picture which will then be published in a future edition.

The clinical section of the April edition opens with a paper which demonstrates how child psychotherapists have applied key concepts to new ways of working over the last decade.

Letter to the Editors from Dr Sara Klaniczay, Budapest, Hungary

Dear Editors,

In this letter I would like to offer a brief summary of the history of child analysis in Hungary. As it is only a letter and not an academic paper, personalities and ideas are referred to without aiming at completeness. I should also say that child psychoanalysis is only a part of the history of psychoanalysis in Hungary and should be seen as being deeply embedded in the historical and social circumstances of the period. Let me call your attention to Pál Harmat's book Freud Ferenczi und the ungarische Psychoanalyse (Edition Discord, Tubingen, 1988), which has served as a source for this letter and sets it in a proper context.1

We Hungarians take pride in the fact that one of the great figures of child analysis, Melanie Klein (1882-1960) was born in Hungary and that her method of therapeutic work was nourished by Ferenczi's ideas and their personal relationship. In 1919, after delivering the lecture entitled ‘The Development of a Child’, she became a member of the Hungarian Psychoanalytical Association. Soon after that she moved to Berlin where she established her practice and began scientific research, settling in Britain some years later.

Child analysis, as it developed in Hungary, however, did not strictly follow Melanie Klein but was based rather on Anna Freud's work, and, on the whole, used a combination of both methods (e.g., therapeutic play has always been an important part of our work). However, the scope of the Budapest School and of child analysis in Hungary has a special feature, having been considerably widened by Imre Hermann's ‘theory of clinging’. Just as Melanie Klein had done, Hungarian child analysts have always studied the early mother-child relationship and the characteristics of the pre-Oedipal period, but in the light of this theory of clinging.

Prenatal experience; separateness; container/contained; sound; psychoanalytic psychotherapy.

This paper describes certain difficulties encountered in patients whose verbal communications can be considered incomplete or distorted. Using Maiello's (1995) concept of a ‘sound-object’ and her ‘musical vertex’ of analytic listening, I explore how the varieties of sound both in utero and postnatally may have their counterpart in our work. Detailed clinical material from the psychotherapy of a selectively mute, 5–year-old girl and the dream of a phobic, young woman in psychoanalysis are presented to demonstrate how their intolerance to my presence/absence is linked to the lack of a particular kind of containment. Both patients suffered the pre- and/or peri-natal loss of their primary object, leading to a stark awareness of otherness (absence/nothingness) without the mitigating confidence of thereness (presence/being). Using Anzieu's (1989) idea of a ‘sound envelope’, I consider how the need for a ‘background object’ that provides a ‘certainty of continuity of contact’ originates in the background noises of the mother's body in utero, and calls for a rhythmicity and attention to ‘symbol and sound’ both postnatally and in our work with such patients.

When a patient says that he knocks on wood three times before every car journey in order to prevent an accident, we do not conclude that he is exploiting an extraordinary kind of causality. When a patient announces that he is Jesus Christ, we do not marvel at a non-standard form of personal identity. But, according to Hanna Segal, when a patient explains that he will not play the violin in public because the performance would be tantamount to masturbation, we should understand that he is employing a peculiar kind of symbolism.

A symbol is one thing that represents another very different thing: for example, the Union Jack is a symbol of the United Kingdom, a particular ring is a symbol of a marriage, a rainbow can be regarded as a symbol of hope (the pot of gold). In ‘“The Importance of symbol-formation in the development of the ego” in context’ (This Journal Vol. 24, No. 3, 1998), Segal repeats the claim made in her influential paper, ‘Notes on symbol formation’ (1957), that there is a form of disturbed symbolization which consists in one thing being treated as identical to a very different thing. Her ‘elementary example’ of symbolic equation is: a doctor asks a schizophrenic patient in a mental hospital why he, the patient, has stopped playing the violin; and the patient replies, ‘Why?, do you expect me to masturbate in public?’ Segal asserts without argument that the patient equates violin with penis and playing the violin with masturbating. But there are outstanding questions. Is this schizophrenic patient incapable of sarcasm, or of angry contempt for what he has valued? Is the patient revealing a loss of competence by expressing his anxiety about being found out, about being the object of ridicule, about feeling shame? Evidently we must not construe the reply as a joke because it was made ‘with some violence’.1 Segal says that ‘the symbol-substitute is felt to be the original object. The substitute's own properties are not recognized or admitted’ (1957). Really? How far does the ‘non-differentiation between the thing symbolized and the symbol’ go? Did the patient become confused when, say, he had to urinate?

Psychosomatic symptoms, embodiment, affect, countertransference use, neurosis and psychosomatic symptoms, borderline and psychosomatic symptoms,

In the treatment of patients with psychosomatic symptoms, the restoration of the link with the affectively experienced body is of crucial importance. The affectively experienced body is the seat of emotional life and the basis upon which words and language can process the meaning of emotions.

We will focus on the restoration of the link with the affectively experienced body in a neurotic patient and in a patient with a borderline character structure. In the course of the therapeutic process, intense countertransference feelings, often experienced on a bodily level, are important indications of the aspects of affective life that have been ejected or foreclosed by the patient with psychosomatic symptoms. If the therapist can contain the primitive affects that have been ejected by the patient, then these affects can be ‘digested’ and given back or communicated to the patient in a tolerable and meaningful way. Thus, the patient can reintegrate aspects of his affective life and rebuild the link with the bodily seat of his affects.

Becoming (re)connected with ‘the affectively experienced body’ is a therapeutic process with significant differences on the neurotic and pre-neurotic levels. Restoring the link with the affectively experienced body for the child with a neurotic character coincides with repairing the contact with the self; for the child with the borderline patterns, it gradually helps to build up this contact with the self.

For psychoanalytic theory, this emphasis on embodiment or ‘bodiliness'1 and affect is of crucial importance in that it completes an emphasis on finding words for affects. An interplay of restoring the link with the affectively experienced body – in itself a process in which language plays an important part – and finding words for what is felt on a bodily level enriches

Parent-child psychotherapy, internal world, reparation, projections, parental feelings,

This paper describes the brief psychotherapy treatment of two families of children under 5 years of age. Each treatment addresses the problems of early childhood in the context of the family relationships and dynamics. The presenting problems are the severe uncontrollability and defiance of the child towards the mother in the first family and the child's soiling as a form of unconscious protest in the second family.

Technical issues are discussed in the context of the clinical material. One key technique described is the exploration of the parental feelings, in order to facilitate the parents' understanding of the emotional link between themselves and their child. Another technique discussed is the gathering of the family history and a picture of the presenting symptoms in the here and now of the sessions. The use of the interpretation of both the family dynamics and the interplay of mutual projections among the family members and the therapist, to increase awareness and modify family interactions, is also discussed.

Holding, letting go, separation, ending therapy, new relationship with therapist, transitions, paradox,

In this paper, the process of ending therapy is likened to the ordinary developmental task of ‘letting go’ that parents have to undertake, to help their child to grow up. ‘Letting go’ is contrasted with the process of ‘holding’ the child in mind that is so central to the therapeutic and parental task. Following thoughts about some of the external issues that play a part in the decision to end a child's treatment, this developmental perspective of psychoanalytic psychotherapy is discussed through a clinical illustration of the ending of a 5–year-old boy's treatment. Different strands of the therapeutic relationship as highlighted during the ending phase of therapy are distinguished and attention is drawn to the role of the ‘new relationship’ between therapist and child and how this differs from the transference relationship. Countertransference issues in their broadest form are also considered.

Endings arouse deepseated anxieties and hence this topic tends to be neglected. In this paper, I show the importance of including a seminar on the subject of ending therapy in the curriculum of training of child psychotherapists. Different kinds of endings and how they are dealt with, indications of the patient's readiness to end, transference and counter-transference issues in the ending period and post-analytic contact are discussed. The Challenges and Struggles of Single Parenthood from a Psychoanalytic Perspective

Judith Edwards

Judith Edwards

36 Ansleigh Place

Judith Edwards   Child and adolescent psychotherapist working in a family consultation centre in the voluntary sector in North London. She teaches on courses at the Tavistock Clinic and in Bristol, and is currently joint editor of the Journal of Child Psychotherapy. Recent publications include chapters in Autism and Personality (see Alvarez, above) and The Handbook of Child and Adolescent Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy (Routledge, 1999).
Single parents, psychotherapy, internal space, Oedipus complex, identification,

The issue of the growth of single-parent families has been in the forefront of political, social and moral debate in recent years. Children from single-parent families tend to be over-represented in clinic populations. Yet this state of family being may be no more potentially pathological than the nuclear family, which can become conceptually idealized. The aim of this paper is to look behind the statistics and examine the impact on children of life in a single-parent family, to explore how this may be managed, and to look for potentiating factors which can enable good-enough development to unfold. Case material is used to illustrate the theme.

Stanley Greenspan is an eminent psychiatrist, professor and psychoanalyst based in Washington who has written prolifically, this being his twenty-eighth book. He writes in the introduction that he is aiming to present a ‘new developmental theory that unifies and extends the practice of psychotherapy’ (p. 1). His own psychoanalytic base seems to be contemporary Freudian, and his psychoanalytic theories are framed within this tradition and its language. However, he sees the aim of this book as partly to challenge the hegemony of any particular theoretical framework and to attempt an integration of psychotherapeutic techniques as diverse as self-psychology, object relations, supportive therapies, short-term therapies and even behavioural techniques. Indeed questions of technique and ‘tactics' are at the heart of the book, and specifically the myriad possible interventions from which we are called upon to choose in each moment of a therapeutic encounter. Greenspan is particularly keen to warn against the ways in which we may defensively use overly well-worn interventions at inappropriate junctures. In numerous detailed case examples he focuses particularly on therapies that fail or reach an impasse because the therapist has been insufficiently aware of the specific developmental stage a patient is at. Indeed, the notion of developmental levels is Greenspan's organizing principle, around which his theories are based.

In the first chapter he outlines his ‘principles of developmentally based psychotherapy’. He states his aim of harnessing a number of what he terms core developmental processes. These have to do with the capacities for self-regulation, forming intimate relationships, engaging in boundary-defining gestures, representing internal experience such as wishes and affects, and being able to differentiate between these internal representations and to build bridges between them. Other clinicians better known to this journal, such as Alvarez (1992), have argued that we have to modify our techniques for particularly deprived and damaged children. However, Greenspan goes further and argues that most patients, adult and children, have considerable developmental deficits, and this requires that we find different technical responses. Problems such as an inability to regulate mood, impulses or to represent affects are, he argues, not simply regressions from more advanced states of ego organization, but actual developmental deficits or constrictions.

The following is an account of the first year of a therapy carried out in the public sector of a child born at the beginning of 1990 in an eastern European country and brought up in a home for abandoned children until he was placed with Italian parents at the end of 1995. I shall describe the child's initial psychological state, vigorous, but desperate, and then go on to describe the course of the first year of therapy, focusing in particular on the sessions of the first period, in which, apart from the quality and intensity of his anxiety, his need to face this anxiety by retracing the stages of his first object experiences is dear.

This paper underlines and explores the connections between emotional and cognitive development at a very early stage, starting from the psychoanalytic psychotherapy of a 4–year-old boy with autistic features. Development of the personality and development of the mind are shown to proceed together and to be interwoven when the therapist starts to help the child to modulate the terror and the rage related to separation. The development of the idea of a good nipple and the introjection of it as a mental structure is considered an important step on the way towards separation between mother and baby and towards the formation within the baby's self of a space where symbols of the external world can be placed. Autistic features are considered as an extreme form of denial of both internal and external reality.

Dr Roger Money-Kyrle's work on cognitive development was essential to the ideas expressed in this paper.

Judy Shuttleworth   Head of Child & Adolescent Psychotherapy in a community-based multi-disciplinary child and adolescent mental health service in North London. She has developed a particular interest in linking psychoanalytic thinking and clinical practice to a multi-causal model of developmental pathology. She has been involved with others in developing multi-disciplinary local services for children with pervasive developmental disorder. She is a teacher and supervisor at the Tavistock Clinic and also teaches in Italy.
Asperger's syndrome, psychoanalytic psychotherapy, narcissism,

This paper describes a lengthy period of psychotherapy with a child. This treatment began only after a prolonged contact with other child and adolescent mental health services during which the child's difficulties, which had initially seemed to be ordinary behavioural problems, had proved puzzlingly intractable to a variety of interventions. Subsequent psychotherapy revealed a profound disorder of development which lay beneath the surface presentation. In a climate where Asperger's syndrome is often felt to be untreatable, this paper argues that some children, at least, can benefit from psychotherapy and can be helped towards real mental growth. Asperger's syndrome in children bears some striking similarities to narcissistic personality disorder as described in the adult psychoanalytic literature and this paper discusses some of the theoretical and clinical implications of the innate origins of Asperger's syndrome.

Following the publication of Anne Alvarez’ paper ‘Failures to link attacks or deficits'? (Vol. 24 No. 2, August 1988), we asked Edna O'Shaughnessy for her views on this subject, and she suggested this format in order to explore the issue of frustration from different theoretical and clinical viewpoints. In this symposium the authors look at the core concept of frustration from Freud's original formulations of the pleasure principle and the reality principle, through Melanie Klein's and Anna Freud's extensions of this and Winnicott's precise distinction between the failure of libidinal satisfaction and the failure of the environment to offer something needed for development. Bion's taking forward of the concept in terms of its centrality in the development of thinking itself in turn paves the way for contemporary thinkers and practitioners to marry the insights of infant observation and child development research. This does not offer an alternative to previous thinking but presents a fuller picture which has both technical and theoretical implications. Clinical material is used by each author to illustrate their theme.

Anne Alvarez Replies

I was interested to learn of the views of Gerland and Sainsbury on Live Company. I was sorry, however, that they saw my book as representative of Bettelheim's view on aetiology, since I thought I had been careful to argue against a simplistic environmental aetiology. Also, I was sorry that they saw it as representative of a traditional psychoanalytic perspective: the book was an account of my struggle to understand precisely why certain traditional psychoanalytic ideas were inadequate in the treatment of people with autism of Robbie's type. I certainly did not write the book to show that psychoanalysis is the only way of understanding and treating autism. On the contrary, I was exploring why some of the traditional psychoanalytic theories and techniques were not helpful with Robbie's autism. I tried to show that a model of the mind which concentrates too much on the concepts of 1) defence against anxiety, 2) resistance and 3) withdrawal as intentionally motivated was often unhelpful for people who have deficits in the capacity for interpersonal relatedness and in symbolic functioning. I came to learn, for example, that Robbie was more undrawn than withdrawn. In the case of some of the non-autistic but nevertheless severely damaged children described in the second part of the book, I suggested that such a model was at times even harmful (at other moments, it was essential). So I am in many ways in considerable agreement with Gerland and Sainsbury.

However, in the book I did go on to point out that psychoanalysis itself has changed greatly in the last century, that modern ideas make much less use of a defence model – some American analysts, for example, insist that a concept of deficit must accompany the concept of defence (Kohut, 1985) and the work of Winnicott (1958) and Bion (1962) in the UK has led to much less emphasis on explanatory interpretations and more on slow careful description and containment – helping thoughts to become thinkable (what Alan Schore (1998; see also 1994) has more recently called ‘structuring the unconscious as opposed to making the unconscious conscious'). I tried to show that these ideas had much relevance for work with people with autism, who, as Gerland and Sainsbury point out, have difficulty in finding words for feelings. I added, however, that even these modern ideas might need supplementing with other ideas, in particular those derived from infant developmental psychology. I tried to give many examples of techniques which did seem to produce more emotional contact and mentalization as compared to those which did not.

Gianna Williams describes the central theme of her book in the first few lines of her introduction as ‘the theme of the impairment in taking in from another, in internalising dependent relationships'. These concepts are the building blocks, a son of primary alphabet out of which, in different combinations, the narrative of the book originates and develops.

One can make a broad central distinction within the impairment of the capacity to establish a vital relationship of dependence on another. On the one hand, are the situations of deprivation or trauma which have either prevented the development of internal structures or overwhelmed them with intolerable input. On the other, are the pathologies where dependency is actively rejected by a turning to destructive internal structures and parts of the self. This distinction is not, however, clear-cut, as the author illustrates in the chapter ‘Doubly deprived’. Here she describes the interplay between external deprivation and the deprivation derived from the development of crippling defences which perpetuate, internally, the experience of actual emotional deprivation.

However, the distinction is useful in identifying the primary function which brings about the development of a specific edifice of defences, in some cases it is a protection from psychic fragmentation; that is, the result of an attempt to survive in a predicament of extreme deprivation or threat, thus acting on the side of life and survival. On the other side of the divide are the defences arising from an abandonment of hope as well as those arising from the mental pain implicit in dependency upon a unique, precious and irreplaceable object.

The author states that the purpose of this book is to offer some important truths about lone twins whose experiences she believes have not been sufficiently understood or validated. The book is the outcome of Woodward's ‘Bereaved Twin Study’ in which she interviewed 219 lone twins, documenting personal accounts of their bereavement and tapping into a rich seam of emotional experiences. The documentation was divided into three categories: 1) those who had lost a twin at birth, 2) in childhood and 3) in adulthood. The evidence, although anecdotal, is gripping and convincing.

Following her interviews, Woodward then invited twenty-five of her subjects to meet together to discuss their experiences. One lone twin said: ‘Difficulties coping with loss and separation in lone twins were too common to be coincidence. I'm sure some people who are not lone twins also have difficulties with separation and loss, perhaps deriving from other factors in their personal history, but I'm convinced that the extent of the desperation which lone twins seem to feel regarding loss and the number of people at the meeting who expressed such intense feelings cannot be coincidental’ (p. 48).

Joan Woodward is a lone twin and it was through her own soul-searching that she embarked on this project. Following the sudden death of her twin sister at 4 years of age she refused to go out of the house and her mother took her to see a child psychoanalyst. Woodward subsequently trained as a psychotherapist but felt no more satisfied that Freudian psychoanalysis understood the lone twin dimension than she had, as a child, felt understood by the child psychoanalyst. She felt she needed to find an alternative theoretical framework to comprehend her loss. She found that Bowlby's attachment theory stood up to the rigorous examination of the many twins' responses to their losses and also provided pointers to helpful therapeutic interventions missing in traditional psychoanalysis.

The study focused on how twins actually experienced their loss and how they would categorize the severity of their loss for themselves. She tried to ascertain what were the worst aspects of their loss and if anything had helped to ameliorate it. Generations of students at the Tavistock have greatly benefited from Margot Waddell's lectures on personality development. The publication of this book is a happy event, allowing us and a wider public to have access to these riches and her further thoughts on the subject. Based on the original psychoanalytic discoveries of Freud, those of Klein and post-Kleinians, drawing on many years of experience of clinical work, added to by observation of babies, children, adolescents and adults and inspired by literary sources, she now presents us with a cohesive picture of inner growth.

The story of how we grow is, as she states in her introduction, ‘not told in orthodox developmental terms, nor yet as a comprehensive view of how, expositionally, psychoanalytic theory would explain such matters. It has come to our attention that views in Britain on the aetiology and treatment of autism are not homogeneous. While psychiatrists, researchers and other professionals involved in diagnosing, educating and providing other services for autistic people are generally up-to-date in their knowledge of the scientific evidence, there are still some psychoanalysts who believe that psychoanalysis is an appropriate treatment for autism. Both of us have been formally diagnosed with high-functioning autism or Asperger's syndrome. As such, we would like to claim the ‘right to reply’ to recent psychoanalytic writings about autism, of which we take Anne Alvarez's Live Company: Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy with Autistic, Borderline, Deprived and Abused Children (1992) to be representative. We feel that such writings not only ignore scientific research into autism, but also disregard and obscure the real experiences and feelings of people with autism.

Alvarez's book centres around the case of ‘Robbie’. This is typical of psychoanalytic writings on autism, which rely on case-histories, rather than scientific data to support their theories; the best-known example of this is Bruno Bettelheim's The Empty Fortress (1967), which is based entirely around case histories. This strategy could have two purposes: either to demonstrate the validity of the psychoanalytic method by showing its effectiveness in a given case or to persuade the reader of the accuracy of the psychoanalyst's understanding and interpretation of this particular patient's experiences.
